title: Training and office hours

story: The pull request for RH-1234, the "No projects yet" card, came with two new tests, and both were green: "the empty table shows a message" and "a filter with no match shows a message". Dana, the teammate who reviewed it, saw the green checks and approved.

A month later, a refactor of the filter code makes a search with no match show "No projects yet" instead of "No results". Users think their projects are gone. The test called "a filter with no match shows a message" is still green, because there is still a message; it never asked which one. The test was there, it was named after exactly this case, and it could never have failed for this bug.
hook.question: How do you know that a check could really have caught the bug it is named after?

read.h: A green test is also a claim
p: We ask for proof instead of claims in every pull request, and a passing test feels like proof. It is proof only of one thing: that this test passes on this code. Whether the test would fail if the behaviour broke is a separate question, and the green check does not answer it.

Look at the two tests from the story. assert.ok passes for any value that is not empty, so "No results", "No projects yet" and "Loading…" all pass. The test checks that something is there, not that the right thing is there. This is called a weak assertion, and it is the most common way a test ends up unable to fail. Others are a test that never reaches the changed code, or a mock that answers whatever the test expects.

notes.text: Passes for any message at all, so it cannot tell No results from No projects yet.
Named after the filter case, but it would pass with the wrong message too.

read.h: Plant a bug, watch it fail, revert
p: The habit that answers the question is small. After a check passes, break your own change on purpose in one small place: flip a condition, swap a return value, change a number. Run the check. If it fails, it covers that behaviour. Then revert the planted bug, so it never ships, and write one line in the pull request about what you planted and how the check failed. If the check still passes, it does not cover your change, and you need a better check before anyone can trust it.

Here the planted bug makes the filter case return the empty-workgroup message, which is exactly the refactor from the story. The weak tests stay green. The strong tests compare the exact message with assert.equal, and the C2 test fails, showing what it expected and what it got.

notes.text: The exact message, so any other text fails.
Names the wrong answer too: the filter case must not show the empty card.

read.see:
not ok 2 - C2 a filter with no match shows No results, not the empty card
  expected: 'No results'
  actual: 'No projects yet'
# pass 1
# fail 1

p: A failure counts only when it comes from an assertion about the behaviour, the line that compares expected with actual. If the planted change breaks an import and the test file crashes with a SyntaxError, every test fails, and it proves nothing about whether any of them checks the right thing. So plant the bug inside the logic the check is about, and read why the check failed, not only that it failed.

The same rule works in the other direction for a brand-new test. Before the feature exists, the test should fail on its assertion, because the behaviour is missing; that is the "before" proof. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, does exactly this: its harness, the program that runs the agent on its machine, runs every new check on the unchanged code first, and each one must fail on an assertion before any product code is written. After the change, a planted bug shows the check still has teeth.

deeper.h: Go deeper: mutation testing does this for you
p: Planting one bug by hand checks one behaviour. Mutation testing tools plant hundreds: they make small changes to your code automatically, such as > into >=, true into false, or a deleted line, run the tests after each one, and report every changed version, called a mutant, that no test noticed. A surviving mutant is a planted bug your tests did not catch. Stryker does this for JavaScript and TypeScript, mutmut for Python.

Line coverage cannot see this problem. The weak tests in this lesson run every line of the filter code, so coverage says 100%, while the wrong message still passes. Coverage tells you which lines ran; a planted bug tells you whether the tests would have noticed a change there.

lab.title: Plant a bug and see which tests notice
lab.goal: Run a weak and a strong test against the projects table logic, plant the bug from the story, see which tests notice, and write the missing edge-case check so a second planted bug is caught too.

guess.q: You change the filter case to return "No projects yet" instead of "No results". Which tests fail: the weak ones that use assert.ok, or the strong ones that use assert.equal?

options.text: Both, because the behaviour is wrong
options.why: assert.ok only asks whether a message exists, and one still does.
It compares the exact message, so the wrong text fails. The weak tests and the strong C1 test stay green.

options.text: None, because the code still runs without errors
options.why: A good test fails on a wrong result, not only on a crash.

follow.say: Write the table logic for RH-1234 and both kinds of test, and commit, so you can always go back to the real code with git.
Plant the bug from the story: the filter case now shows the empty-workgroup message. Run the weak tests first.
follow.do:
sed -i '' 's/return { message: "No results", rows: \[\] }/return { message: "No projects yet", rows: [] }/' table-view.mjs
git diff --stat
node --test weak.test.mjs 2>&1 | grep -E '^# (pass|fail)'
follow.see:
table-view.mjs | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
# pass 2
# fail 0

follow.say: Now the strong tests, on the same broken code. Read why C2 failed: expected against actual.
follow.see:
not ok 2 - C2 a filter with no match shows No results, not the empty card
  expected: 'No results'
  actual: 'No projects yet'
# pass 1
# fail 1

follow.say: Revert the planted bug, so it can never ship, and confirm everything is green again.

lab.build: The plan's third check, C3, has no test yet: with 1,000 projects, the first page shows 25 rows. First plant a bug for it: change PAGE_SIZE = 25 to PAGE_SIZE = 50 and run node --test. Every test passes, so nothing covers C3. Revert it. Write c3.test.mjs that builds 1,000 projects, calls tableView, and checks with assert.equal that there are 25 rows and that the first row is Project 1. Run it (green), plant PAGE_SIZE = 50 again (it must fail with expected: 25, actual: 50), and revert. Finish by writing the one line you would put in the pull request about each planted bug.
checks: The planted message bug left the weak tests green and failed the strong C2 test with expected 'No results', actual 'No projects yet'.
PAGE_SIZE = 50 passed every test before you wrote c3.test.mjs.
c3.test.mjs passes on the real code and fails on PAGE_SIZE = 50 with expected: 25 and actual: 50.
git diff is empty at the end: no planted bug is left in table-view.mjs.
You wrote one line per planted bug, such as: Planted: C2 shows No projects yet; C2 failed (expected No results).
lab.fix: A teammate says they proved C1 and C2 can fail: they renamed export const tableView to tableVeiw, ran node --test strong.test.mjs, and both tests failed. Do the same and read the output: SyntaxError: The requested module './table-view.mjs' does not provide an export named 'tableView'. Explain why this failure proves nothing about either check, revert it, and plant one bug per check that fails on its assertion instead.
explain: Why does the weak C2 test stay green when the filter shows the wrong message?
What should you do when a planted bug does not make your check fail?
Why does a failure from a broken import not count as proof that a check can fail?
lab.done: Every check C1 to C3 has failed once on its own assertion because of a bug you planted, all bugs are reverted, and the suite is green.

check.q: You plant a small bug in your change, flipping one condition, and the test for that behaviour still passes. What does that tell you?

options.text: The bug you planted is harmless, so the change is safe to ship
options.why: You changed the behaviour on purpose. A test that did not notice is the problem, not the bug.

options.text: The test does not cover your change, so you need a better check before anyone can trust it
options.why: A check proves something only if it can fail. This one could not, for the very change it is named after.

options.text: The planted bug was too small; plant a bigger one until the test fails
options.why: A bigger break, such as a crash, would fail the test for the wrong reason and hide the gap.

check.q: Your planted change breaks an import, and every test in the file fails with a SyntaxError. Is that proof that the tests can catch bugs?

options.text: No: they failed because the file could not load, not because an assertion saw wrong behaviour
options.why: Proof needs an assertion comparing expected with actual. A crash says nothing about what the test checks.

options.text: Yes: every test failed, which is even stronger proof
options.why: More failures from one crash prove less, not more; they would fail the same way with no assertions at all.

options.text: Yes, as long as you revert the change afterwards
options.why: Reverting keeps the bug out of main, but it does not make the failure meaningful.

check.q: After the check fails on your planted bug, why do you revert it and write one line about it in the pull request?

options.text: So the git history stays short
options.why: The line goes in the pull request description, not in the history. The reason is the reviewer.

options.text: So CI can skip that test next time
options.why: CI runs every test every time. The planted bug is a one-time proof, not a setting.

options.text: So the bug never ships, and the reviewer can see each check could fail without planting bugs themselves
options.why: The line turns a green check into proof: this check failed when the behaviour broke.

p: This lab is the core of the first of four trainings for every engineer: checks before code, proof not claims. In 45 minutes, people see a pull request with proof next to one with claims, then plant a bug in a small real bug fix (one frontend and one backend exercise on seed data in FCP Lab, the full product on one machine) and watch a weak test stay green. The second training is plan mode and the grill, with pairs reviewing each other's checks; the third is running many agents at once (worktrees, background agents, one writer per change, and a size and token estimate in the prompt for people's own sessions); the fourth is working with Nova, from assigning a ticket to reviewing its draft pull request.

From week 6 to week 12 a 30-minute weekly office hour answers questions about skills, plugins and agents, alternating between Shai and Platform, with the Harness Lab course offered as self-study. Every session is recorded and linked from a brain page, and the questions people struggled with become eval cases (Training 1 feeds verify, Training 2 feeds plan-and-grill), skill lines or brain pages; the top three themes go to the weekly run review.

tickets.why: Training 1: checks before code, a planted bug, proof for the PR; its hardest questions become verify eval cases.
Training 2: plan mode and plan-and-grill with two real tickets.
Training 3: many agents at once, sized on purpose.
Training 4: handing work to Nova and reviewing its pull requests.
Weekly office hours and the question log that feeds the tools.

words.plain: A small change you make on purpose to your own code, to see whether a check notices, then revert.
A test line that passes for many wrong results, such as checking that a message exists instead of which one.
Fail because a comparison of expected and actual was wrong, not because the code crashed.
Tools that plant many small bugs automatically and report the ones no test noticed (surviving mutants).

review.q: From memory: the four steps of the planted-bug habit.
review.a: Break one small thing in your change, run the check and see it fail on its assertion, revert, and write one line in the pull request about what you planted and how it failed.

review.q: A test has 100% line coverage of the filter code but uses assert.ok on the message. Is it a good test? How do you find out quickly?
review.a: Not necessarily: coverage shows the lines ran, not that the test would notice a wrong result. Plant a bug, such as the wrong message, and see whether it fails.

remember: A check proves something only if it can fail: plant a small bug, see it fail on its assertion, revert, and say so in the pull request.
